Test Case: AWS smoke test passes (aws_local)
What This Checks: Checks that Zamboni can reach every AWS service it needs (Glue, Athena, S3, SNS, DynamoDB) plus its own database.
Before You Start: .env.aws_local is set up. You have run aws sso login (or the setup script).
Steps: Run: python scripts/aws_smoke_test.py --create-lock-table --init-control-plane-db
What Should Happen: All 8 checks say PASS. Exit code is 0. Last line says 'All checks PASSED or SKIPPED cleanly.'

Test Case: AWS smoke test passes on the real EC2 server
What This Checks: Same checks as SMK-01, run from the real EC2 server using its own permissions.
Before You Start: App is deployed to EC2. The .env file points the database at /data/zamboni/zamboni_control.db.
Steps: Log into the server (SSM or SSH). Run: cd /opt/zamboni && .venv/bin/python scripts/aws_smoke_test.py --json
What Should Happen: The database check passes because the path starts with /data/zamboni, not /opt/zamboni. All other checks pass too.

Test Case: Smoke test blocks a database path inside /opt/zamboni
What This Checks: Checks that Zamboni refuses to start if its database is stored in a folder that gets wiped on every deploy.
Before You Start: Running on EC2.
Steps:
In the shell only (do not edit the real .env file), set:
ZAMBONI_CONTROL_PLANE_DB=/opt/zamboni/zamboni_control.db
Then run: python scripts/aws_smoke_test.py
Undo the change afterward.
What Should Happen: The database check FAILS with a clear warning about /opt/zamboni. The whole command exits with an error.

Test Case: Lock table creation is safe to repeat
What This Checks: Checks that the lock table (stops two jobs touching the same table at once) is created safely, and running the setup twice does not break anything.
Before You Start: None.
Steps:
Run: python scripts/aws_smoke_test.py --create-lock-table
Run it again a second time.
Then: aws dynamodb describe-table --table-name zamboni_maintenance_locks
What Should Happen: The table exists with the right key and a TTL setting. The second run just says it already exists.

Test Case: Old leftover AWS keys don't block real login
What This Checks: Checks that an old, expired AWS key sitting in your terminal does not stop Zamboni from using your real login.
Before You Start: Working from a laptop (aws_local mode).
Steps:
Set a fake/old AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY in your shell.
Run: python scripts/aws_smoke_test.py
What Should Happen: The identity check still PASSES, using your real SSO login, not the old fake keys.

Test Case: Database setup can run more than once safely
What This Checks: Checks that setting up the database is safe to run again without causing errors.
Before You Start: None.
Steps:
Run: python scripts/init_control_plane_db.py
Run it again right after.
What Should Happen: First run says some updates were applied. Second run says 0 new updates and confirms everything looks correct.

Test Case: Discover finds only real Iceberg tables
What This Checks: Checks that scanning a database only picks up real Iceberg tables and skips other table types.
Before You Start: A Glue database with at least one Iceberg table (use the test-table script if you don't have one).
Steps: Run: python -m engine.cli.register discover --db <database> --out test_manifest.yaml
What Should Happen: The counts on screen are correct. The output file lists only the Iceberg tables, each with sensible defaults.

Test Case: Bulk register dry run changes nothing
What This Checks: Checks that a dry run of bulk registration does not change the database.
Before You Start: You have the file from REG-01.
Steps:
Run: python -m engine.cli.register bulk --manifest test_manifest.yaml (dry run is the default).
Then check: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM stream_registry WHERE table_fqn LIKE 'glue_catalog.<db>.%'
What Should Happen: Screen shows 'DRY RUN' for each table. No new rows appear in the database.

Test Case: Bulk register for real saves the tables
What This Checks: Checks that a real (non-dry-run) bulk registration actually saves the tables and applies a policy.
Before You Start: REG-02 is done.
Steps:
Run: python -m engine.cli.register bulk --manifest test_manifest.yaml --no-dry-run (confirm yes).
Check stream_registry and hk_config for the new tables.
What Should Happen: Screen shows 'REGISTERED'. Each table now has one row in stream_registry and one matching row in hk_config.

Test Case: Registering the same table twice does not duplicate it
What This Checks: Checks that registering the same table twice does not create duplicate rows.
Before You Start: REG-03 is done.
Steps: Run the exact same command again: python -m engine.cli.register bulk --manifest test_manifest.yaml --no-dry-run
What Should Happen: Screen shows 'SKIP (already registered)' for every table. No extra rows are added.

Test Case: Registering one table picks a sensible policy automatically
What This Checks: Checks that registering one table on its own picks a sensible policy template automatically.
Before You Start: A table Glue knows about that Zamboni hasn't registered yet.
Steps: Run: python -m engine.cli.register single --table <fqn> --domain <domain> --layer staging --tier standard --no-dry-run
What Should Happen: Screen shows the template it picked. hk_config has a row with that template's settings.

Test Case: Status command matches reality
What This Checks: Checks that the status command accurately shows what's registered and what isn't.
Before You Start: A database with some tables registered and some not.
Steps: Run: python -m engine.cli.register status --db <database>
What Should Happen: 'Registered' and 'Unregistered' counts add up to the real number of Iceberg tables. The unregistered list is correct.

Test Case: Enable/disable HK for a domain works, dry run first
What This Checks: Checks that turning housekeeping on or off for a whole domain works, and a dry run changes nothing first.
Before You Start: Some tables registered under a test domain.
Steps:
Run: python -m engine.cli.enable --domain <domain> --layer staging (dry run, check the preview looks right).
Run again with --no-dry-run (confirm).
Check: SELECT table_fqn, hk_enabled FROM stream_registry WHERE domain='<domain>'
What Should Happen: The dry run changes nothing. The real run turns hk_enabled on for every matching table.

Test Case: A future start date puts a table into safe trial mode
What This Checks: Checks that setting a future start date puts a table into a safe trial period without fully turning housekeeping on.
Before You Start: A registered table.
Steps: Run: python -m engine.cli.enable --table <fqn> --dry-run-until 2026-08-01 --no-dry-run
What Should Happen: The table's dry_run_until date is set. hk_enabled stays as it was. A run before that date only simulates -- it makes no real changes.

Test Case: Applying a template fills in the right settings
What This Checks: Checks that applying a policy template fills in the correct settings for a table.
Before You Start: A registered table with no policy set up yet.
Steps:
In a Python shell:
from engine.core.config import apply_template
apply_template(table_fqn='<fqn>', template_name='STAGING_DEFAULT', dry_run=False)
Then check the hk_config row.
What Should Happen: The table's gates, schedule, and compaction settings match the STAGING_DEFAULT template exactly.

Test Case: Sort columns are saved as plain text
What This Checks: Checks that the list of sort columns is saved correctly as plain text (an older bug saved it in a format the database couldn't read).
Before You Start: A template or table using sort or zorder compaction, with sort columns set.
Steps:
Apply a template with sort_columns set to two column names on a table.
Check: SELECT sort_order_cols FROM hk_config WHERE table_fqn='<fqn>'
What Should Happen: The value is plain comma-separated text. The save does not fail.

Test Case: Manual override has a time limit and is logged
What This Checks: Checks that a manual override (to skip the conflict check for a short time) has a maximum length and is logged.
Before You Start: A registered table.
Steps:
Set an override on the table for 2 hours, with a reason and your name.
Run: python -m engine.scripts.run_hk --table <fqn> --no-dry-run
What Should Happen: The log shows the override was used, with your reason and name. The run skips the live conflict check while it's active. An override set further out than the allowed limit gets shortened, not rejected.

Test Case: Busy tables get a safer retention floor than quiet ones
What This Checks: Checks that busy tables (lots of writes per day) get a shorter, safer snapshot-retention floor than quiet tables.
Before You Start: A table with a known write pattern, or a test table with many recent inserts.
Steps:
In a Python shell:
from engine.core.commit_frequency import get_commit_stats
print(get_commit_stats('<fqn>'))
What Should Happen: The tier (HIGH, MEDIUM, or LOW) matches how often the table is really written to. Vacuum never sets a retention floor shorter than that tier allows.

Test Case: Dry-run preview shows the correct plan
What This Checks: Checks that the dry-run preview command shows the correct plan without changing anything.
Before You Start: A domain with a mix of tables that would run and tables that would be skipped.
Steps: Run: python -m engine.cli.dry_run --domain <domain> --verbose
What Should Happen: Each table's gate results and run/skip verdict match its real settings. The SQL preview shown is valid Athena SQL. Nothing in the database changes.

Test Case: A self-conflicting schedule is rejected
What This Checks: Checks that you can't save a schedule that blocks its own start time.
Before You Start: None.
Steps: Try to save a schedule that starts at 07:00 with a blocked window of 06:00-09:00, using the Policy page or PUT /api/policies/{fqn}.
What Should Happen: The save is rejected with a clear error. Nothing is saved.

Test Case: Zamboni detects AWS's own auto-optimizer running
What This Checks: Checks that Zamboni notices when AWS's own auto-optimizer is already turned on for a table, which would conflict with Zamboni's own housekeeping.
Before You Start: Turn on one AWS Glue table optimizer (for example, compaction) on a test table, using the AWS Glue console.
Steps:
In a Python shell:
from engine.core.conflict_detector import check_table
print(check_table('<fqn>'))
What Should Happen: The result says conflict=True and names which optimizer is on.

Test Case: A conflict check result is remembered for a while
What This Checks: Checks that Zamboni reuses a recent conflict check instead of asking AWS again every time.
Before You Start: GT0-01 was just run.
Steps: Call the cached check again right away and compare the saved check-time before and after.
What Should Happen: The second call reuses the saved answer. The check-time does not change, meaning AWS was not asked again.

Test Case: Scanning many tables for conflicts is efficient
What This Checks: Checks that scanning many tables for conflicts saves results in batches, not one save per table.
Before You Start: More than 25 registered tables.
Steps:
In a Python shell:
from engine.core.conflict_detector import scan_fleet
print(scan_fleet())
Watch how many Athena queries run while it works.
What Should Happen: Roughly one save per 25 tables, not one per table. Every table's conflict flags are still updated correctly.

Test Case: A conflicting table is skipped by housekeeping
What This Checks: Checks that housekeeping actually skips a table when AWS's own optimizer is already on for it.
Before You Start: GT0-01's conflicting table. No active override.
Steps: Run: python -m engine.scripts.run_hk --table <fqn> --no-dry-run
What Should Happen: The run exits normally. The log shows the table was skipped because of the AWS conflict. No compaction or vacuum ran.

Test Case: An override lets the run go ahead despite a conflict
What This Checks: Checks that turning on an override lets the run go ahead even with a conflict present.
Before You Start: The same conflicting table as GT0-04.
Steps:
Set an override 2 hours into the future, with a reason.
Run: python -m engine.scripts.run_hk --table <fqn> --no-dry-run
What Should Happen: The log shows the override was used, with your reason. The run moves on to the next checks instead of skipping.

Test Case: Only one process can hold a table's lock
What This Checks: Checks that only one process can hold the lock on a table at a time.
Before You Start: None.
Steps:
Window 1, Python shell:
from engine.core.lock_service import LockService
ls = LockService()
l = ls.acquire('<fqn>', 'test')
Window 2, at the same time:
LockService().acquire('<fqn>', 'test2')
What Should Happen: Window 1 gets the lock. Window 2 gets nothing back, because the lock is already held.

Test Case: An expired lock can be taken over
What This Checks: Checks that a lock frees itself automatically once it times out, so a crashed job can't hold a table locked forever.
Before You Start: A lock acquired with a very short timeout (ttl_min=0), or wait past the normal lock timeout.
Steps: Get a very short-lived lock. Wait about a minute. From a second window, try to get the lock again.
What Should Happen: The second attempt succeeds once the first lock has expired.

Test Case: A long job keeps its lock alive the whole time
What This Checks: Checks that a long-running job keeps its lock alive the whole time it's working, instead of losing it partway through.
Before You Start: None.
Steps:
Get a lock, then start its heartbeat.
Wait a couple of minutes.
Check the lock's expiry time before and after.
What Should Happen: The expiry time keeps moving forward roughly every 60 seconds. A different process still cannot grab the lock the whole time.

Test Case: Losing the lock mid-run stops the job safely
What This Checks: Checks that if a job loses its lock mid-run, it stops itself before doing anything destructive, instead of continuing unprotected.
Before You Start: A housekeeping run in progress on a table.
Steps: While the run is going, force-release its lock from another window (or call DELETE /api/locks/{fqn}) to simulate the lock being stolen. Watch what the first run does.
What Should Happen: The run fails safely as soon as it notices the lock is gone. It does not finish the vacuum, optimize, or delete step after that point.

Test Case: An admin can force-clear a stuck lock
What This Checks: Checks that an admin can manually clear a stuck lock.
Before You Start: A lock left behind by a crashed process (for example, from GT0-06).
Steps:
Force-release the lock (admin action, or DELETE /api/locks/{fqn}).
Confirm it's gone by listing locks.
What Should Happen: The lock is gone. A new attempt to get the lock on that table now succeeds right away.

Test Case: Housekeeping waits for the upstream job to finish
What This Checks: Checks that housekeeping waits for the upstream Control-M job to finish before touching a table.
Before You Start: Table has Gate 1 turned on, pointing at a Glue job that's still running or hasn't run today.
Steps: Run: python -m engine.scripts.run_hk --table <fqn> --no-dry-run
What Should Happen: The log shows the run was skipped because the upstream job isn't done yet. Nothing runs on the table.

Test Case: Housekeeping proceeds once the upstream job finishes
What This Checks: Checks that housekeeping proceeds once the upstream job has finished.
Before You Start: Same table as GT1-01, after the upstream job has succeeded.
Steps: Run again: python -m engine.scripts.run_hk --table <fqn> --no-dry-run
What Should Happen: The run moves past this check instead of skipping.

Test Case: Turning off Gate 1 skips the upstream check
What This Checks: Checks that turning Gate 1 off skips the upstream-job check entirely.
Before You Start: Same table, Gate 1 turned off, upstream job still not finished.
Steps: Run: python -m engine.scripts.run_hk --table <fqn> --no-dry-run
What Should Happen: The run does not wait for the upstream job at all.

Test Case: Dry-run preview shows the true upstream job status
What This Checks: Checks that the dry-run preview shows the true, current status of the upstream job.
Before You Start: Any table with Gate 1 turned on.
Steps:
Run: python -m engine.cli.dry_run --table <fqn>
Compare to: aws glue get-job-runs --job-name <job>
What Should Happen: The Gate 1 column on screen matches the real job status in AWS.

Test Case: A table is skipped outside its scheduled window
What This Checks: Checks that a table with a fixed schedule is skipped outside its allowed time window.
Before You Start: The current time is outside the table's schedule.
Steps: Run: python -m engine.scripts.run_hk --table <fqn> --no-dry-run
What Should Happen: The log shows the run was skipped for being outside its window. Nothing runs.

Test Case: A blocked hour stops the run even inside the window
What This Checks: Checks that a blocked-hours setting stops a run even if it's technically inside the normal window.
Before You Start: The current hour falls inside the table's blocked hours.
Steps: Run during a blocked hour: python -m engine.scripts.run_hk --table <fqn> --no-dry-run
What Should Happen: The log shows the run was skipped for being in a blocked hour.

Test Case: A wrong day of the week is skipped
What This Checks: Checks that a schedule limited to certain days of the week is skipped on other days.
Before You Start: Table's schedule only allows certain days.
Steps: Run on a day it's not allowed: python -m engine.scripts.run_hk --table <fqn> --no-dry-run
What Should Happen: The log shows the run was skipped for being the wrong day.

Test Case: Force run overrides the schedule
What This Checks: Checks that a manual force-run setting overrides the schedule.
Before You Start: A table currently outside its window (like GT2-01).
Steps:
Turn on force_run for the table.
Run: python -m engine.scripts.run_hk --table <fqn> --no-dry-run
What Should Happen: The run goes ahead even though it's outside the normal window.

Test Case: Turning off Gate 2 skips the schedule check
What This Checks: Checks that turning off Gate 2 skips the schedule check entirely.
Before You Start: Same outside-window table, Gate 2 turned off.
Steps: Run: python -m engine.scripts.run_hk --table <fqn> --no-dry-run
What Should Happen: The run goes ahead no matter what the schedule says.

Test Case: 3 failures in a row turns housekeeping off
What This Checks: Checks that a table gets automatically turned off after failing 3 times in a row.
Before You Start: A test table you can make fail on purpose (for example, point it at a Glue job that doesn't exist).
Steps: Run: python -m engine.scripts.run_hk --table <fqn> --no-dry-run three times, so each one fails.
What Should Happen: After the 3rd failure, the table's housekeeping is switched off automatically, with a clear reason, and an alert is sent.

Test Case: Turning housekeeping back on alone doesn't clear a lockout
What This Checks: Checks that simply turning housekeeping back on does not undo a failure lockout by itself.
Before You Start: GT3-01's table, turned back on again right away.
Steps: Run: python -m engine.scripts.run_hk --table <fqn> --no-dry-run
What Should Happen: The run is still skipped, because there were 3 failures within the last 30 days. Turning it back on alone does not clear this.

Test Case: One serious failure can also trip the breaker
What This Checks: Checks that one serious data-integrity failure switches off housekeeping right away, without needing to fail 3 times.
Before You Start: A situation that causes one integrity check to fail (for example, the lock-loss situation from GT0-09).
Steps:
Trigger one run that fails its integrity check.
Check the table's housekeeping setting right after.
What Should Happen: Housekeeping is switched off after this single failure, not after three.

Test Case: An alert is actually sent when a table trips
What This Checks: Checks that an alert really gets sent when a table gets switched off.
Before You Start: A working email or Slack subscription on the alerts topic.
Steps:
Trigger GT3-01 or GT3-03.
Watch the subscribed inbox or channel.
What Should Happen: An alert naming the table and the reason arrives within a couple of minutes.

Test Case: Recovery needs old failures to age out, not a manual reset
What This Checks: Checks that a table only becomes runnable again once its old failures are more than 30 days old -- there's no manual reset button.
Before You Start: GT3-02's still-blocked table.
Steps: Wait until the 3 failures are more than 30 days old (or, only for testing, backdate them in a throwaway copy of the data). Run the table again.
What Should Happen: Once fewer than 3 failures remain in the last 30 days, the table runs normally again.

Test Case: Running the same table twice doesn't do the work twice
What This Checks: Checks that running the same table twice in the same window doesn't repeat the work.
Before You Start: A table that already ran successfully once this window.
Steps: Run: python -m engine.scripts.run_hk --table <fqn> --no-dry-run twice, right after each other.
What Should Happen: The second run is skipped as a duplicate. Nothing runs twice.

Test Case: Two different triggers for the same job don't double up
What This Checks: Checks that two different triggers for the same table and time window are treated as the same job, so they don't double up.
Before You Start: None.
Steps:
In a Python shell:
from engine.core.idempotency import build_execution_id
print(build_execution_id('run-A', '<fqn>', 'hk_run', '<window_id>'))
print(build_execution_id('run-B', '<fqn>', 'hk_run', '<window_id>'))
What Should Happen: Both lines print the exact same ID, even though the run names are different.

Test Case: A completed run is remembered by other processes too
What This Checks: Checks that a completed run is remembered even by a completely different process.
Before You Start: None.
Steps:
In one Python session, mark a run as done.
In a brand-new session, check if it's already done.
What Should Happen: The second, separate session correctly sees the run as already done.

Test Case: A healthy table is left alone
What This Checks: Checks that a healthy table with nothing to fix is left alone.
Before You Start: A table that was just compacted and vacuumed.
Steps: Run: python -m engine.scripts.run_hk --table <fqn> --no-dry-run
What Should Happen: The log shows the table was skipped as healthy. No changes were made.

Test Case: Dry run makes zero changes even when work is needed
What This Checks: Checks that a dry run truly makes zero changes, even when real work is needed.
Before You Start: A test table with lots of small files or snapshots.
Steps:
Note the snapshot and file counts.
Run: python -m engine.scripts.run_hk --table <fqn> --dry-run
Check the counts again.
What Should Happen: The log shows what WOULD happen, but the real counts on the table don't change at all.

Test Case: A real run shrinks the number of small files
What This Checks: Checks that a real run actually reduces the number of small files (compaction).
Before You Start: A test table built with lots of small inserts.
Steps:
Note the file count. In Athena: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM "<table>$files"
Run: python -m engine.scripts.run_hk --table <fqn> --no-dry-run
Check the file count again.
What Should Happen: The file count drops a lot. The log shows the compaction step succeeded and passed its checks.

Test Case: Vacuum cleans up old snapshots and stray files together
What This Checks: Checks that vacuum removes both old snapshots and stray orphan files in one step.
Before You Start: A test table with planted orphan files and enough history to need cleanup.
Steps:
Run: python -m engine.scripts.run_hk --table <fqn> --no-dry-run
Check the vacuum_audit table for this run.
What Should Happen: The audit row shows it wasn't aborted, the snapshot count went down, and the old orphan files were deleted. The log shows the vacuum step passed its checks.

Test Case: Brand-new orphan files are never deleted
What This Checks: Checks that orphan files under 72 hours old are never deleted, even by vacuum.
Before You Start: A test table with orphan files planted in the last hour.
Steps:
Run housekeeping right after planting the files: python -m engine.scripts.run_hk --table <fqn> --no-dry-run
Check S3 before and after.
What Should Happen: The freshly planted files are still there afterward. They're too new to be touched.

Test Case: Vacuum refuses to delete too much at once
What This Checks: Checks that vacuum refuses to run if it looks like it would delete too much at once -- a safety check against something going badly wrong.
Before You Start: A table where almost all its snapshots look ready to expire.
Steps: Run: python -m engine.scripts.run_hk --table <fqn> --no-dry-run
What Should Happen: The audit row shows it was aborted, with a reason. No real deleting happened. The table's housekeeping gets switched off and an alert is sent.

Test Case: A failed settings update stops the run instead of guessing
What This Checks: Checks that if Zamboni can't safely set the table's vacuum settings first, it stops instead of guessing and going ahead anyway.
Before You Start: A situation where the settings update can be made to fail (for example, remove the test account's permission to update the table).
Steps:
Cause the settings update to fail.
Run: python -m engine.scripts.run_hk --table <fqn> --no-dry-run
What Should Happen: The run stops before vacuum runs at all. Nothing on the table is touched. Restore the permission afterward.

Test Case: Zamboni double-checks its settings actually took effect
What This Checks: Checks that Zamboni confirms its settings really took effect, not just that the update call didn't error.
Before You Start: None specific -- this happens on every real run.
Steps: After any real housekeeping run, compare the table's real settings in Glue against what Zamboni intended to set.
What Should Happen: The real settings on the table exactly match what Zamboni asked for.

Test Case: An unclear result is marked failed, not verified
What This Checks: Checks that if Zamboni can't fully confirm a table's before/after state, it reports the run as failed, not as verified.
Before You Start: None -- review recent run history.
Steps: Look through the execution log for rows where the before or after snapshot info is blank.
What Should Happen: Any such row is marked as failed, never marked as verified.

Test Case: A table isn't re-run before its next scheduled turn
What This Checks: Checks that a table isn't re-run before its next scheduled turn comes up.
Before You Start: A table that just ran successfully.
Steps: Run it again immediately: python -m engine.scripts.run_hk --table <fqn> --no-dry-run
What Should Happen: The run is skipped as not due yet.

Test Case: Zamboni backs off when Athena is already busy
What This Checks: Checks that Zamboni waits, or backs off, when Athena is already busy, instead of piling on more work.
Before You Start: Several long queries already running in the same Athena workgroup.
Steps: While Athena is busy, run: python -m engine.scripts.run_hk --table <fqn> --no-dry-run
What Should Happen: The step waits, and skips if things stay busy too long. Nothing is submitted while Athena is saturated. It works normally once things free up.

Test Case: The older housekeeping path still works as a fallback
What This Checks: Checks that the older, simpler housekeeping path still works if the newer one is switched off.
Before You Start: None.
Steps:
Turn off the new path: set ORCHESTRATED_MAINTENANCE=false
Run: python -m engine.scripts.run_hk --table <fqn> --no-dry-run
Turn it back on afterward.
What Should Happen: The run completes using the older code path instead.

Test Case: A fleet-wide run only touches the right tables
What This Checks: Checks that a fleet-wide run only touches tables that are actually turned on for the right environment.
Before You Start: A mix of on/off tables across two environments.
Steps: Run: python -m engine.scripts.run_hk --domain <domain> --environment <env> --dry-run
What Should Happen: The number of tables processed exactly matches the tables turned on for that domain and environment. No others show up in the log.

Test Case: The command reports failure correctly
What This Checks: Checks that the command's exit code correctly reports success or failure.
Before You Start: At least one table set up to fail.
Steps:
Run: python -m engine.scripts.run_hk --domain <domain> --no-dry-run
Check the exit code afterward.
What Should Happen: Exit code is 1 if anything failed, 0 if everything went fine.

Test Case: The 'how busy is Athena' count matches reality
What This Checks: Checks that Zamboni's count of how many queries are running matches reality.
Before You Start: 2-3 long queries running in a workgroup (start them manually in the Athena console).
Steps:
In a Python shell:
from engine.core.backpressure import get_running_query_count
print(get_running_query_count('app'))
What Should Happen: The number printed matches what you see running in the Athena console.

Test Case: A failed busyness check doesn't get Zamboni stuck
What This Checks: Checks that if the 'how busy is Athena' check itself fails, Zamboni carries on instead of getting stuck.
Before You Start: Temporarily remove permission for the busyness check.
Steps: With the permission removed, run: python -m engine.scripts.run_hk --table <fqn> --no-dry-run
What Should Happen: The run still goes ahead, even though the busyness check itself couldn't work. Restore the permission afterward.

Test Case: Dry-run archiving shows the plan without moving data
What This Checks: Checks that a dry run of archiving shows what would move, without moving anything.
Before You Start: A table with archiving turned on and at least one old partition.
Steps: Run: python -m engine.scripts.run_archival --domain <domain> --dry-run
What Should Happen: The summary shows partitions found. No new files appear in S3. The source data is untouched.

Test Case: A real archive run moves data to S3 and removes it from the live table
What This Checks: Checks that a real archive run moves old data to S3 and removes it from the live table.
Before You Start: Same as ARC-01.
Steps:
Run: python -m engine.scripts.run_archival --domain <domain> --no-dry-run
Check the archive bucket and the source table.
What Should Happen: The data is now in the archive bucket. The source partition is empty. The log shows success with real bytes archived.

Test Case: Archiving refuses to delete data written after export
What This Checks: Checks that archiving refuses to delete a partition if new data was written to it after the export, so nothing is silently lost.
Before You Start: A partition being archived, with a way to write a new row into it mid-run.
Steps: Start an archive run. Insert a new row into the exact partition being archived, between the export and delete steps.
What Should Happen: Archiving notices the mismatch and refuses to delete. The log explains why.

Test Case: Archiving and housekeeping can't touch the same table at once
What This Checks: Checks that archiving and housekeeping can't both touch the same table at the same time.
Before You Start: None.
Steps: Hold a lock manually on a table. At the same time, run: python -m engine.scripts.run_archival --domain <domain> --no-dry-run for that table.
What Should Happen: Archiving skips or waits for that table instead of running at the same time as the lock holder.

Test Case: Archiving stops safely if it loses its lock mid-batch
What This Checks: Checks that archiving also stops safely if it loses its lock partway through a batch of partitions.
Before You Start: A table with several partitions to archive at once.
Steps: Force-release the archive job's lock mid-run from another window. Watch what happens to the remaining partitions.
What Should Happen: Every remaining partition's delete step is blocked once the lock is confirmed lost, not just the one that noticed first.

Test Case: The command reports failure correctly
What This Checks: Checks that the command's exit code correctly reports success or failure.
Before You Start: A partition set up to fail (for example, remove S3 write permission).
Steps:
Run: python -m engine.scripts.run_archival --domain <domain> --no-dry-run
Check the exit code.
What Should Happen: Exit code is 1. Restore the permission afterward.

Test Case: Reported storage savings match what's really in S3
What This Checks: Checks that the reported storage savings match what's actually in S3.
Before You Start: ARC-02 is done.
Steps: Compare: aws s3 ls --summarize --human-readable on the archive folder, against the total bytes archived in the log.
What Should Happen: The two numbers roughly match.

Test Case: Scanning finds non-prod tables and adds them to tracking
What This Checks: Checks that scanning finds non-prod tables and adds them to the tracking list.
Before You Start: A non-prod database with Iceberg tables, under an active domain.
Steps: Run: python -m engine.scripts.run_lifecycle_scan --environment preprod --no-dry-run
What Should Happen: New rows appear for these tables, all starting in the ACTIVE state.

Test Case: Scanning skips databases with no active domain
What This Checks: Checks that scanning skips a database whose domain isn't registered or is turned off, so it's never even looked at.
Before You Start: A non-prod database whose domain has no record, or is turned off.
Steps: Run: python -m engine.scripts.run_lifecycle_scan --environment preprod --no-dry-run
What Should Happen: No new tracking rows appear for that database's tables at all.

Test Case: An unused table becomes a stale candidate
What This Checks: Checks that an inactive table moves from ACTIVE to STALE_CANDIDATE after being unused long enough.
Before You Start: A table that hasn't been queried or written to in a long time.
Steps: Run: python -m engine.scripts.run_lifecycle_cycle --environment preprod --no-dry-run
What Should Happen: The table's state changes to STALE_CANDIDATE.

Test Case: The owner is notified before the grace period starts
What This Checks: Checks that the owner is emailed or alerted BEFORE a table's grace period starts, not after.
Before You Start: LFC-03's table. A working subscription on the greenzone alert topic.
Steps: Run again: python -m engine.scripts.run_lifecycle_cycle --environment preprod --no-dry-run
What Should Happen: A notification is received. The table only moves to GREENZONE, with a 14-day grace period, after that notification succeeds.

Test Case: A failed notification stops the table from moving forward
What This Checks: Checks that if the notification fails to send, the table does NOT quietly move forward anyway.
Before You Start: Notifications temporarily broken (for example, an invalid alert address) for a table about to change state.
Steps: Run: python -m engine.scripts.run_lifecycle_cycle --environment preprod --no-dry-run with notifications broken.
What Should Happen: The table's state does not change. The log shows the notification failed. Fix notifications afterward.

Test Case: A table moves to pending-drop once its grace period ends
What This Checks: Checks that a table moves from GREENZONE to PENDING_DROP once its grace period runs out, with one last warning sent.
Before You Start: LFC-04's table, with its grace period backdated or waited out.
Steps: Run: python -m engine.scripts.run_lifecycle_cycle --environment preprod --no-dry-run
What Should Happen: The table's state changes to PENDING_DROP, with a 2-day countdown. A final warning is received.

Test Case: Exempting a table keeps it safe permanently
What This Checks: Checks that marking a table exempt keeps it safe from deletion, permanently.
Before You Start: A table in GREENZONE or PENDING_DROP.
Steps:
Mark it exempt.
Run the scan and cycle scripts a few more times.
What Should Happen: The table stays ACTIVE and marked exempt, even though it's still genuinely unused.

Test Case: Claiming a table is temporary, not permanent
What This Checks: Checks that claiming a table (instead of exempting it) is temporary -- it can become stale again later.
Before You Start: A table in STALE_CANDIDATE or GREENZONE.
Steps: Claim it. Confirm it's ACTIVE and not exempt. Let it sit unused again and re-run the cycle.
What Should Happen: The table becomes STALE_CANDIDATE again eventually, unlike an exempted table, which never would.

Test Case: Backup-named tables are flagged automatically
What This Checks: Checks that backup-style tables (named _bkp, _backup, or _copy) get flagged automatically.
Before You Start: A non-prod table with one of these names.
Steps: Run: python -m engine.scripts.run_lifecycle_scan --environment preprod --no-dry-run
What Should Happen: That table is flagged as a backup-pattern table.

Test Case: Cleanup really deletes an expired table (TEST TABLES ONLY)
What This Checks: Checks that cleanup really deletes an expired table, from both Glue and S3. Use a disposable test table only.
Before You Start: A disposable test table pushed into PENDING_DROP with its countdown already expired.
Steps: Run: python -m engine.scripts.run_cleanup --environment preprod --no-dry-run
What Should Happen: The table is gone from Glue. Its S3 data is gone. The tracking row shows DROPPED, with storage reclaimed. It shows up in Deletion History.
Environment: Both -- test tables only, never a real project table

Test Case: Cleanup re-checks a table right before deleting it (TEST TABLES ONLY)
What This Checks: Checks that cleanup double-checks a table's state right before deleting it, in case someone exempted it moments earlier.
Before You Start: Two expired test tables queued for cleanup.
Steps: Start cleanup. The moment it begins, exempt one of the two tables from another window, before cleanup reaches it.
What Should Happen: The exempted table is spared. The other one is still deleted normally.

Test Case: Cleanup refuses to delete if the domain got turned off (TEST TABLES ONLY)
What This Checks: Checks that cleanup refuses to delete a table if its domain got turned off after the table was marked for deletion.
Before You Start: An expired test table whose domain is currently active.
Steps:
Turn the domain off right before or during the run.
Run: python -m engine.scripts.run_cleanup --environment preprod --no-dry-run
What Should Happen: The table is skipped, not deleted. Turn the domain back on and confirm a later run does delete it (as a sanity check).

Test Case: Cleanup also respects the table lock (TEST TABLES ONLY)
What This Checks: Checks that cleanup respects the table lock, like housekeeping and archiving do.
Before You Start: None.
Steps:
Hold a lock manually on an expired test table.
Run: python -m engine.scripts.run_cleanup --environment preprod --no-dry-run
What Should Happen: That table's delete is skipped or delayed instead of happening at the same time as the lock holder.

Test Case: Dry-run cleanup deletes nothing
What This Checks: Checks that a dry-run cleanup deletes nothing.
Before You Start: An expired PENDING_DROP test table.
Steps: Run: python -m engine.scripts.run_cleanup --environment preprod --dry-run
What Should Happen: The table still exists in Glue and S3 afterward. Screen shows what WOULD be deleted.

Test Case: Saving a new non-prod table doesn't silently fail
What This Checks: Checks that saving a newly-found non-prod table works correctly, and doesn't silently fail.
Before You Start: A brand-new non-prod table never seen by a scan before.
Steps: Run: python -m engine.scripts.run_lifecycle_scan --environment preprod --no-dry-run twice in a row.
What Should Happen: Both runs report zero errors. The table ends up with exactly one row, not zero and not two.

Test Case: All three lifecycle commands report failure correctly
What This Checks: Checks that all three lifecycle commands correctly report failure when something goes wrong.
Before You Start: A domain with a table set up to fail.
Steps:
Run each of the three lifecycle scripts against it.
Check the exit code after each.
What Should Happen: Exit code is 1 whenever a table failed.

Test Case: Rollback lists real, past versions of a table
What This Checks: Checks that the rollback tool lists real, previous versions of a table's metadata.
Before You Start: A table with at least 2 completed housekeeping runs.
Steps: Run: python scripts/recover_metadata.py --fqn <fqn> --dry-run
What Should Happen: The list shows real, past metadata locations, newest first.

Test Case: Rollback refuses a target that doesn't exist
What This Checks: Checks that the rollback tool refuses a target file that doesn't actually exist.
Before You Start: None.
Steps: Run: python scripts/recover_metadata.py --fqn <fqn> --to s3://<bucket>/bogus.metadata.json --dry-run
What Should Happen: It says the target is invalid, with a clear reason. It exits with an error. Nothing in Glue changes.

Test Case: A dry-run rollback changes nothing
What This Checks: Checks that a dry-run rollback changes nothing.
Before You Start: A valid rollback option exists for a table.
Steps: Run: python scripts/recover_metadata.py --fqn <fqn> --dry-run (pick a target, give a reason).
What Should Happen: Screen says 'DRY RUN -- no changes made'. The table's real metadata pointer is unchanged. A log entry is still recorded.

Test Case: A real rollback only changes the metadata pointer (TEST TABLE ONLY)
What This Checks: Checks that a real rollback only changes the metadata pointer, and leaves every other table setting untouched.
Before You Start: A valid rollback option on a disposable test table.
Steps:
Note all of the table's current settings first.
Run: python scripts/recover_metadata.py --fqn <fqn> --no-dry-run (type the table name to confirm).
Check the settings again.
What Should Happen: Only the metadata pointer changed. Everything else is identical. An alert is sent. A log entry is recorded.

Test Case: A wrong confirmation name blocks the rollback
What This Checks: Checks that typing the wrong table name at the confirmation step blocks the rollback.
Before You Start: A valid rollback option exists.
Steps: Run: python scripts/recover_metadata.py --fqn <fqn> --no-dry-run and type the wrong name when asked to confirm.
What Should Happen: It says the confirmation didn't match, and stops. Nothing changes in Glue.

Test Case: App changes are instantly visible to the engine
What This Checks: Checks that a change made through the app is instantly visible to the engine, with no delay.
Before You Start: The main database is set up.
Steps:
Change a domain's name through the app or API.
Right after, check it from Python using the engine's own read function.
What Should Happen: The engine sees the new value immediately, with no waiting or refreshing needed.

Test Case: Engine-owned columns stay only in the cloud, not the local copy
What This Checks: Checks that a few special columns (owned by the engine, not the app) are kept only in the cloud table, not copied into the local database.
Before You Start: None.
Steps:
List the columns in the local stream_registry table.
Compare to the columns in the cloud version.
What Should Happen: The engine-owned columns (like AWS-conflict flags) exist in the cloud version but not in the local one.

Test Case: Background sync copies changes to the cloud on schedule
What This Checks: Checks that the background sync job actually copies changes from the local database to the cloud on schedule.
Before You Start: The sync service is running, or run it once by hand.
Steps:
Change a domain's name through the app.
Wait for a sync cycle (or run scripts/control_plane_sync.py once by hand).
Check the cloud copy directly.
What Should Happen: The cloud copy shows the change after the sync runs. Special engine-owned columns are kept, not wiped out.

Test Case: Sync refuses to wipe cloud data from a suspiciously empty local copy
What This Checks: Checks that sync refuses to wipe out real cloud data if the local database looks suspiciously empty. Use a throwaway copy of the database for this test.
Before You Start: A table with real data already synced to the cloud. A spare, throwaway copy of the local database file.
Steps: On the throwaway copy only, delete all rows from one table, then try to sync it to the real cloud table.
What Should Happen: Sync refuses and sends an alert instead of wiping out the cloud data. A special setting is needed to force it through on purpose.

Test Case: Backups are saved to S3 and can be checked before restoring
What This Checks: Checks that scheduled backups are saved to S3 and can be checked before restoring.
Before You Start: The backup service is running, or run it once by hand.
Steps:
Confirm a new backup file appears in S3.
Run: python scripts/control_plane_restore.py --latest --dry-run
What Should Happen: The backup shows up right away. The dry-run preview correctly picks the newest one and makes no changes.

Test Case: Restoring refuses a broken backup file
What This Checks: Checks that restoring refuses a broken or unreadable backup file, without touching the real database.
Before You Start: Upload a deliberately broken file to the backups folder in S3.
Steps: Run: python scripts/control_plane_restore.py --key <bad-key> --dest ./scratch_restore_test.db (use a throwaway file path).
What Should Happen: It refuses the backup with a clear error. The throwaway file is left empty or missing. Delete the bad test file afterward.

Test Case: The daily health check notices real corruption
What This Checks: Checks that the daily health check on the database notices real corruption and sends an alert.
Before You Start: A throwaway, deliberately damaged copy of the database file.
Steps:
Point the database setting at the damaged throwaway copy.
Run: python scripts/control_plane_integrity_check.py
What Should Happen: It reports a failure with details, exits with an error, and sends an alert. Switch back to the real database path afterward.

Test Case: An empty database auto-restores from the latest backup
What This Checks: Checks that if the database ever comes up empty, Zamboni automatically restores it from the latest backup.
Before You Start: A throwaway, empty database path. At least one real backup exists in S3.
Steps:
Make sure the throwaway path doesn't exist yet.
Run: python scripts/init_control_plane_db.py pointed at it.
What Should Happen: It says it auto-restored from a backup. The tables now have real data, not empty ones.

Test Case: Zamboni refuses to start silently empty
What This Checks: Checks that Zamboni refuses to start with a silently-empty database, unless someone confirms that's expected.
Before You Start: No backups exist yet for a throwaway test path.
Steps: Run: python scripts/init_control_plane_db.py against the empty, backup-free path.
What Should Happen: It refuses to continue and explains why, instead of quietly starting empty.

Test Case: A first-install setting acknowledges a genuinely new setup
What This Checks: Checks that there's a deliberate way to confirm 'yes, this really is a brand-new setup' when there's no backup.
Before You Start: Same empty, no-backup situation as CP-09.
Steps:
Turn on the 'first install' setting.
Run: python scripts/init_control_plane_db.py again.
What Should Happen: It proceeds and clearly says this was acknowledged as a first-time setup. Turn the setting back off afterward.

Test Case: Database updates apply exactly once and don't half-finish
What This Checks: Checks that database updates only apply once, and a failed update doesn't leave things half-changed.
Before You Start: None for the normal case. A throwaway copy missing one column, for the failure case.
Steps:
Run the setup script on an up-to-date database (expect no changes).
Then run it on a throwaway copy missing a column.
What Should Happen: The up-to-date database reports zero new changes. The throwaway copy gets exactly the one missing piece added, and passes its own check afterward.

Test Case: The database survives a server replacement (DISRUPTIVE)
What This Checks: Checks that the database survives even if the EC2 server itself gets replaced. This is a disruptive test -- plan it deliberately, not during active use.
Before You Start: The app is deployed on EC2.
Steps:
Register a test domain through the app.
Force the server to be replaced (for example, by changing the machine image).
After the new server is up, check for the test domain.
What Should Happen: The test domain is still there -- the storage survived the replacement instead of starting empty.

Test Case: Cost report totals match a manual check
What This Checks: Checks that the cost report's totals match a manual check of the raw data.
Before You Start: Some completed runs exist with recorded data-scanned amounts.
Steps:
Run: python -m engine.cli.cost_report --days 30
Separately, add up the same numbers directly from the log table.
What Should Happen: The two totals match.

Test Case: Exporting the cost report to a file works
What This Checks: Checks that exporting the cost report to a CSV file works.
Before You Start: None.
Steps: Run: python -m engine.cli.cost_report --export cost_test.csv
What Should Happen: The file exists, opens cleanly, and matches what's on screen.

Test Case: Fleet coverage percentage is calculated correctly
What This Checks: Checks that the fleet coverage percentage is calculated correctly.
Before You Start: A domain with a known mix of on/off tables.
Steps:
Run: python -m engine.cli.fleet_status coverage --domain <domain>
Cross-check by counting the tables yourself.
What Should Happen: The printed totals and percentage exactly match your manual count.

Test Case: Never-housekept tables show up on the stale report
What This Checks: Checks that tables which have never been housekept show up on the stale report.
Before You Start: A table that's turned on but has never actually run, or hasn't run in a while.
Steps: Run: python -m engine.cli.fleet_status stale --domain <domain> --days 14
What Should Happen: That table appears on the list. A recently-run table does not.

Test Case: Both log-writing modes produce the same complete results
What This Checks: Checks that the two different ways of writing the run log produce the same complete results.
Before You Start: None.
Steps:
Run one housekeeping cycle with one log-writing mode, and another cycle with the other mode.
Check both sets of log rows.
What Should Happen: Both modes produce complete rows with all the same fields filled in.

Test Case: Saving many log rows at once doesn't drop any
What This Checks: Checks that saving many log rows at once doesn't quietly drop any of them.
Before You Start: None.
Steps:
Run something that logs several steps at once (like a domain-wide dry run).
Check the log for that run.
What Should Happen: The number of log rows matches the number of steps that actually ran -- nothing missing.

Test Case: Alerts go to the most specific matching contact
What This Checks: Checks that alerts go to the most specific matching contact, not a random or overly general one.
Before You Start: A few contact entries set up at different levels of detail for the same domain.
Steps: Look up the contact for different combinations of domain, environment, and tier.
What Should Happen: The most specific matching entry always wins.

Test Case: The weekly summary shows real, accurate numbers
What This Checks: Checks that the weekly summary for a domain shows real, accurate numbers.
Before You Start: A domain with some recent run history.
Steps:
In a Python shell:
from engine.core.digest import build_digest
import json
print(json.dumps(build_digest('<domain>'), default=str, indent=2))
What Should Happen: The numbers (runs, failures, storage saved) match the real log for that domain over the last 7 days.

Test Case: The weekly summary is actually delivered
What This Checks: Checks that the weekly summary email or alert is actually delivered.
Before You Start: A domain with the weekly summary turned on and a working email or alert address.
Steps:
Trigger the weekly summary for that domain.
Check the inbox.
What Should Happen: A message arrives with real numbers for that domain.

Test Case: Lifecycle warnings and safety alerts use separate channels
What This Checks: Checks that lifecycle warnings and safety alerts go to two separate channels, not mixed together.
Before You Start: Subscriptions set up on both alert channels.
Steps: Trigger a lifecycle warning (LFC-04) and a safety alert (GT3-04) around the same time.
What Should Happen: Each message arrives on its own correct channel.

Test Case: The generator refuses to run in production, no way around it
What This Checks: Checks that the test-table generator refuses to run in production, with no way around it.
Before You Start: None.
Steps:
Set your environment to prod.
Run: python scripts/seed_synthetic_iceberg_tables.py --database <db> --s3-location s3://<bucket>/zamboni-test/ --yes
What Should Happen: It refuses immediately and exits with an error, before touching AWS at all. Reset your environment setting afterward.

Test Case: The generator refuses to run in local-only mode
What This Checks: Checks that the generator refuses to run in local-only mode, since there's no real database to create tables in.
Before You Start: Local mode turned on.
Steps: Run: python scripts/seed_synthetic_iceberg_tables.py --database <db> --s3-location s3://<bucket>/zamboni-test/
What Should Happen: It explains there's no real database in this mode and exits.

Test Case: A dry run shows the plan without creating anything
What This Checks: Checks that a dry run just shows the plan, without creating anything.
Before You Start: A dev or preprod environment with a real AWS connection.
Steps: Run: python scripts/seed_synthetic_iceberg_tables.py --database <db> --s3-location s3://<bucket>/zamboni-test/ --num-tables 3
What Should Happen: Screen shows the plan for 3 tables. Nothing new actually appears in the database.

Test Case: A real run creates working test tables with real history
What This Checks: Checks that a real run actually creates working test tables with realistic history.
Before You Start: Same as SYN-03.
Steps: Run: python scripts/seed_synthetic_iceberg_tables.py --database <db> --s3-location s3://<bucket>/zamboni-test/ --num-tables 3 --min-inserts 20 --max-inserts 40 --no-dry-run --yes
What Should Happen: 3 new tables exist, each with roughly as many snapshots as it had inserts.

Test Case: Planted orphan files really appear in S3
What This Checks: Checks that the plant-orphan-files option really adds untracked files to S3.
Before You Start: SYN-04 done, or run fresh with the orphan-files option.
Steps:
Run with --orphan-files 5 --no-dry-run --yes.
Check the table's S3 folder.
What Should Happen: 5 extra junk files exist that aren't part of the real table data.

Test Case: Cleanup removes test tables completely
What This Checks: Checks that cleanup removes the test tables completely, from both Glue and S3.
Before You Start: SYN-04/05 done.
Steps: Run: python scripts/seed_synthetic_iceberg_tables.py --database <db> --s3-location s3://<bucket>/zamboni-test/ --cleanup --no-dry-run --yes
What Should Happen: All the test tables are gone from Glue. Their S3 folders are completely empty, including the planted junk files.

Test Case: All background services are running after a deploy
What This Checks: Checks that all of Zamboni's background services are running after a deploy.
Before You Start: A deploy has just finished.
Steps:
Log into the server and run:
systemctl status zamboni-api zamboni-control-plane-sync zamboni-control-plane-backup zamboni-control-plane-integrity.timer
What Should Happen: All services show as running (or, for the timer, waiting). None have failed.

Test Case: Scheduled jobs actually fire the engines
What This Checks: Checks that the scheduled jobs actually fire the engines automatically.
Before You Start: Scheduling is turned on.
Steps:
Wait for the hourly housekeeping schedule to fire (or trigger it manually).
Check the log file on the server.
What Should Happen: A fresh run shows up in the log at the right time, with a real summary.

Test Case: Turning scheduling off pauses jobs without deleting the schedule
What This Checks: Checks that turning scheduling off pauses the jobs without deleting the schedule itself.
Before You Start: None.
Steps:
Redeploy with scheduling turned off.
Check the schedule's status in AWS.
What Should Happen: The schedule shows as disabled, not deleted. Turning it back on works without needing to recreate anything.

Test Case: Log files rotate properly and get shipped off the server
What This Checks: Checks that log files rotate properly and get shipped off the server.
Before You Start: Services have been running for a while, or force a rotation manually.
Steps:
Force a log rotation.
Check for the rotated file.
Check the cloud logging console for recent entries.
What Should Happen: Old logs get rotated out. New log entries keep appearing. The cloud console shows recent activity.

Test Case: A failed server startup would actually be visible
What This Checks: Checks that a failed server startup would actually be visible, not silent.
Before You Start: None -- just check any running server.
Steps: Look at the BootstrapSuccess metric for the server in the cloud monitoring console.
What Should Happen: It shows a value of 1, recorded at boot time.

Test Case: A second deploy does not wipe out saved data
What This Checks: Checks that redeploying the app a second time does not wipe out the saved data.
Before You Start: At least one deploy already done, with test data saved.
Steps:
Check the server's settings file for the database path.
Trigger a second deploy.
Check the app again for the earlier test data.
What Should Happen: The database path points outside the folder that gets wiped on deploy. All earlier test data is still there after the second deploy.
